strengths: Novel and useful framing: the paper explicitly targets the interaction between a generation policy and a downstream safety classifier as a compound system, rather than treating alignment and filtering as independent problems — an underexplored but practically important setting given real-world deployment architectures (guardrails, content-safety APIs, constitutional classifiers).

The decision-theoretic derivation (Section 3, Proposition 1) gives a clean, intuitive justification for why expected system utility is minimized near the classifier's decision boundary, motivating the proposed reward shape in a principled (if stylized) way.

The proposed reward (Eq. 3) is lightweight, requiring only classifier logits and an existing reward model, and is compatible with standard RL fine-tuning (GRPO) and parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA), making the method practical to apply.

Experiments span multiple model families and scales (0.5B–14B, Qwen2.5 and Gemma-2), and the ablations (guard-only reward, prompt-aware reward) are informative: they show that the reward-model term is not always necessary for larger models, and that naively encouraging 'easier-to-catch' unsafe generations backfires badly, adding nuance beyond the main result.

The failure-mode analysis (Section 6.2.2, Appendix C) with concrete qualitative examples strengthens the diagnostic value of the ablations and demonstrates an honest exploration of when the idea does not work.
weaknesses: No comparison to any existing safety-alignment baseline discussed at length in Section 2 (Safe RLHF, C-DPO, SafeDPO, SACPO, safe-completions/deliberative alignment). The only baselines are the untouched base instruct models and the authors' own ablations, so it is unclear whether Boundary Guidance actually outperforms simpler or already-published alternatives, undermining the significance claim.

Evaluation relies entirely on a single LLM-as-judge (GPT-4.1) with no human verification or inter-rater agreement check, and the same judge is used for both helpfulness and harmfulness scoring on a 1-4 / 0-3 scale that is coarse and could be noisy; there is no discussion of judge calibration or robustness to prompt wording.

Train/test split is drawn from the same three source datasets (jailbreak set, Alpaca, HarmfulQA) used for training, so the reported gains reflect in-distribution generalization only. No evaluation on independent, held-out safety/over-refusal benchmarks (e.g., XSTest, OR-Bench, novel jailbreak families) is provided, leaving open whether the boundary-avoidance behavior transfers to unseen attack types or genuinely novel benign queries, which is the central practical concern for a safety method.

The reward directly optimizes the safety classifier's own confidence score, creating an obvious reward-hacking/adversarial-pressure risk: the policy could learn to produce off-distribution text that pushes the classifier's logit to extremes without being more or less safe in reality. This concern is exactly what the prompt-aware ablation reveals as a failure mode, yet the main experiment does not investigate whether the fine-tuned models are still being scored consistently by the *same* guard classifier used for training versus the independent LLM judge, nor test transferability to a different/held-out classifier.

The decision-theoretic model is quite reductive (binary safety, constant u(x,y), an arbitrary λ=1 assumption, single scalar threshold τ=0.5 not tied to the actual deployed filter threshold), and the paper acknowledges but does not resolve how these simplifications affect the validity of the derived reward in more realistic multi-harm or non-binary settings (deferred to future work).

Statistical reporting uses many paired t-tests across sub-groups/models without correction for multiple comparisons, and some key results (e.g., the 14B model's helpfulness drop, several ablation deltas) are only marginally significant or not significant, which is somewhat glossed over in the narrative (e.g., 'the only utility regression... is statistically insignificant').

Training uses 4-bit quantized LoRA fine-tuning for a single epoch with short (96-token) rollouts, which may bias generation length/content and limits confidence that results would hold under full fine-tuning or with longer, more realistic completions typical of production LLMs.
The paper's own code is not yet linked ("Code available at" is left blank), limiting reproducibility despite claims of comprehensive implementation details.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and underexplored problem: fine-tuning generators in the context of a downstream safety classifier rather than in isolation, which is a practically relevant 'compound system' perspective.
The decision-theoretic framing (Section 3) gives an intuitive, if simple, motivation for why outputs near a classifier's decision boundary can be especially costly in expected utility.

The method itself is lightweight (LoRA fine-tuning, single logit from an existing guard model), making it cheap to apply relative to approaches requiring auxiliary deliberation or additional large models.

Multiple ablations (guard-only reward, prompt-aware reward) are included and show at least some analysis of reward design choices and failure modes (e.g., degenerate refusal, reward hacking by making outputs more detectably unsafe).
weaknesses: The central claim that Boundary Guidance 'reduces false positives and false negatives' of the filter is never directly measured. No false-positive/false-negative rates, ROC-style analysis, or classifier confidence distributions before/after fine-tuning are reported — only LLM-judge helpfulness/harmfulness scores, which is a significant disconnect between the paper's core theoretical claim and its empirical evidence.

Evaluation relies entirely on a single LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) with coarse ordinal scales (1-4 and 0-3) and no human validation, inter-annotator agreement, or check for judge bias/self-preference, undermining the reliability of the reported effects.

The practical reward (Eq. 3) used for training is only loosely connected to the theoretically derived utility (Eq. 1/2): Proposition 1 depends on an unrealistic constant-utility assumption that is never revisited quantitatively, and the actual reward omits the λ, 1, and τ parameters the theory emphasizes as important — weakening the paper's claim that the method is theoretically grounded.

The ablation results undercut the main narrative: the guard-only reward (without the reward model u(x,y)) performs comparably or even better than the full Boundary Guidance method for larger models, directly contradicting the stated theoretical necessity of incorporating utility, yet this tension is not resolved, only noted.

Train and test prompts are drawn from the same three datasets (jailbreak corpus, Alpaca, HarmfulQA) via a simple train/test split, so there is no genuinely out-of-distribution evaluation; it is unclear whether gains generalize beyond the narrow prompt distribution used for RL fine-tuning.

No comparison against any of the extensively reviewed baseline methods (Safe RLHF, C-DPO, SafeDPO, SACPO, safe-completions) is provided, despite the related work section positioning Boundary Guidance against them; this leaves the comparative advantage of the proposed method empirically unsubstantiated.

Reported effect sizes are often small and inconsistent across model scales (e.g., only 2 of 4 models show significant helpfulness gains, and the largest model shows a helpfulness decrease), making the 'Pareto improvement' claim overstated for a method tested on only four base models with a single run each (no seeds/repeats, no variance estimates beyond noisy per-prompt t-tests).

Reproducibility is weak: the code link is left blank ('Code available at'), and key design choices (e.g., why max completion length is capped at 96 tokens, which could materially bias helpfulness judgments toward truncated responses) are not justified or ablated.

The single guard model (Llama-Guard-2) and single reward model (Skywork-Reward-V2) are used throughout; no experiments vary the safety classifier or reward model, so robustness of 'boundary guidance' to different filters — central to its generalizability claim — is unestablished.

Quantization (4-bit NF4) and LoRA fine-tuning are used uniformly without ablating against full fine-tuning, leaving open whether reported effects are partly artifacts of the specific efficient-training setup rather than the reward design itself.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: how to fine-tune generators for compound systems that pair a generation policy with a downstream safety classifier, rather than optimizing the generator in isolation.

Provides a clean, interpretable decision-theoretic argument (Proposition 1) showing that expected system utility can be minimized near the classifier's decision boundary, which motivates the boundary-avoiding reward design in a principled way.

Empirical evaluation spans multiple model families and scales (0.5B to 14B, Qwen2.5 and Gemma-2), and the main result (Figure 2, Table 1) shows a fairly consistent pattern of reduced harmfulness with maintained or improved helpfulness.

The ablation studies are a genuine strength: removing the reward model and adding prompt-awareness both yield instructive negative results (e.g., degenerate refusal collapse on the 0.5B model, and the failure mode where prompt-aware rewards actively train the model to produce more extreme unsafe content), which helps readers understand the mechanism and boundary conditions of the method.

The limitations and future work sections are candid, acknowledging reliance on classifier accuracy away from the boundary, multi-model training overhead, and the oversimplified binary-safety assumption.
weaknesses: The entire evaluation (both helpfulness and harmfulness) is conducted exclusively via a single LLM-as-judge (GPT-4.1) with no human validation, inter-annotator agreement check, or calibration of the judge against ground truth, which is a significant reproducibility/validity concern for a safety-focused claim.

Only one safety classifier (Llama-Guard-2-8B) and one reward model (Skywork-Reward-V2) are used throughout; there is no evidence the approach generalizes to other classifiers/reward models with different calibration properties or decision boundaries, which is important since the method's core assumption is that classifiers are more accurate away from the boundary.

The decision threshold (t=0.5) used to define 'near the boundary' in the reward (Eq. 3) is fixed arbitrarily and not shown to correspond to the classifier's actual calibrated boundary τ; no sensitivity analysis on this threshold is reported.

Several of the 'Pareto improvement' claims are overstated: e.g., Qwen2.5-14B shows a (statistically insignificant) helpfulness decrease, and the ablation on reward-model necessity contradicts the main narrative for the 0.5B model, where removing the reward model causes helpfulness to collapse to 1.40 (versus 2.13 base) — undermining the claim that the reward model is merely 'second-order.'

No comparison against existing safety-aligned fine-tuning baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., Safe RLHF, SafeDPO, or a straightforward 'minimize P(filtered)' reward as actually implemented, not just the paper's own simplified variant) to show Boundary Guidance's advantage over prior approaches empirically rather than only conceptually.

Train/test prompts are drawn from the same three source datasets (jailbreak corpus, Alpaca, HarmfulQA) with only an in-distribution held-out split; there is no out-of-distribution or red-teaming evaluation to test whether the boundary-avoiding behavior generalizes beyond the training distribution's adversarial style.
No code repository link is actually provided (placeholder left empty), undermining the reproducibility claim made in the Reproducibility statement.

Potential reward-hacking risk is only partially explored: the prompt-aware ablation shows the model can learn to produce more extreme harmful content to 'help' the classifier, suggesting the main method could have similar unexamined failure modes under different optimization pressure or longer training.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: treating the generator+filter as a compound system rather than optimizing the generator in isolation against a 'pass the filter' objective is a useful and underexplored angle for safety fine-tuning.

A clean, if simple, theoretical justification (Theorem 1 and Proposition 1) is provided for why pushing classifier scores away from the decision threshold should not decrease compound-system utility under natural monotonicity assumptions.

Reasonably broad empirical study spanning four base models (0.5B to 14B, two model families), multiple ablations (reward-model vs. guard-only reward, prompt-aware reward, weaker classifiers, long-context prompts), which helps characterize when the method helps or fails.

Commendable transparency: the paper includes a judge-robustness check (Gemini vs. GPT-4.1) and openly reports failure modes (e.g., the 0.5B model collapsing to near-universal refusal under guard-only reward, and the prompt-aware reward hurting performance), rather than only presenting favorable results.
The training data mixture (jailbreak, benign, harmful prompts) and evaluation protocol are clearly described, aiding partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Each configuration is trained with only a single run (explicitly acknowledged in Appendix A.1) with no seeds/variance reported for RL fine-tuning, which is known to be high-variance; this substantially weakens confidence that the observed differences reflect the method rather than training noise.

The judge-robustness experiment in Appendix D actually undermines central claims: switching to Gemini-2.5 as judge reverses the helpfulness direction for three of four models (only the 14B model retains a clear Pareto improvement), yet this is relegated to an appendix rather than integrated into the main narrative or resolved.

The theoretical contribution is fairly thin: Theorem 1 is essentially the observation that a pointwise max of two oppositely-monotone functions has a minimum at their crossing point, and the specific reward design m(t)=|t-τ| is only loosely justified as 'the simplest bounded proxy' despite the claim that any monotone transform would work—no ablation over reward-shaping functions is provided.

No comparison against existing safety-alignment baselines discussed in related work (Safe-RLHF, SafeDPO, C-DPO, SACPO, safe-completions) is conducted; all comparisons are fine-tuned vs. the same model's base version, making it hard to assess whether Boundary Guidance offers gains over prior safety fine-tuning approaches.

Pareto improvement does not hold uniformly: results broken down by prompt type (Appendix C) show that for harmful prompts, helpfulness decreases for larger models even though harmfulness also decreases, meaning the central 'Pareto improvement' claim is prompt-mix dependent, a caveat that is somewhat underemphasized in the abstract/main text.

The reliance on training and evaluating with the same classifier (no distribution shift study of train-time vs deployment-time classifier mismatch) leaves a central practical concern about robustness to classifier updates entirely unaddressed except as 'future work', despite this being a core motivation for the method's real-world value.

Some evidence of possible reward/classifier gaming is noted informally (e.g., '0.5B distilling the reward model') but not investigated with mechanistic analysis, leaving open whether reported improvements reflect genuine quality gains or exploitation of the auxiliary models.

Evaluation relies solely on LLM-as-a-judge scoring (GPT-4.1 primary, Gemini secondary) with no human validation or inter-annotator agreement, which is a meaningful limitation given known LLM-judge biases, especially for a safety-critical claim.

strengths: The paper provides a clean decision-theoretic motivation (Theorem 1 and Proposition 1) for why avoiding classifier decision boundaries should improve compound-system utility, giving the method a principled starting point.

The empirical study spans a reasonable range of model families and scales (0.5B–14B, Qwen2.5 and Gemma-2), several safety classifiers of different strength, and several reward formulations, which is a genuine effort at robustness checking.

The authors are commendably transparent about failure modes: the collapse of the 0.5B model to universal refusals under guard-only reward, the failure of the prompt-aware reward variant (with concrete rollout examples in Appendix E), and the sensitivity to weak classifiers.

The paper disaggregates results by prompt type (benign/harmful/jailbreak) and shows the Pareto-improvement claim does not hold uniformly, which is an honest and useful nuance rather than an overclaim in that specific section.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim of the paper is that the 'standard approach' of training the generator to reduce filtering probability pushes samples toward the decision boundary and is therefore suboptimal, yet this naive baseline is never actually implemented and compared against Boundary Guidance empirically. All reported comparisons are against the unfine-tuned base model or against ablations of Boundary Guidance itself, so the paper's core comparative claim is asserted but not empirically demonstrated.

The evaluation relies entirely on LLM-as-a-judge scores (GPT-4.1) with no human verification. When the authors re-run the guard-only experiments with a different judge (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Appendix D), the Pareto-improvement pattern reverses for three of four models (helpfulness decreases), directly contradicting the paper's main claim and the framing in the abstract/Figure 2 that presents the GPT-4.1 results as the headline finding without adequately foregrounding this instability.

Table 7 and Table 8 (per-prompt-type breakdown) show that for harmful-request prompts, helpfulness actually decreases for most models under Boundary Guidance (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B: −0.18, Gemma-2-9B: −0.20, Qwen2.5-14B: −0.33), meaning Pareto improvement holds only for benign and jailbreak subsets. This significant caveat is understated relative to the strong claims in the abstract and Figure 2 caption ('Pareto improvements for most settings').

Training results are based on a single run per configuration (explicitly acknowledged in Appendix A.1), with no seed variation; the reported statistical significance stems only from evaluation-set variance (paired t-tests across prompts), not from variance across training runs, so claims of 'robustness' across scales and reward designs are not well supported statistically.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is essentially the elementary observation that the pointwise maximum of one non-decreasing and one non-increasing function attains its minimum where they cross—a nearly immediate consequence of the definitions—yet it is presented as a principal contribution; it adds limited insight beyond the intuitive motivation already given in the introduction.

The method itself is a very simple reward-shaping term (|t−0.5|) added to an off-the-shelf reward model score; the technical novelty is modest, and the paper's contribution rests almost entirely on the empirical study, which has the issues noted above.

Failure modes (0.5B model collapsing to refusals, sub-1B classifiers degrading helpfulness) suggest the method requires sufficiently capable policy and classifier models to work, limiting the generality of the claimed benefits and raising questions about when practitioners can rely on it.

The training/evaluation prompt mixture (jailbreak dataset, Alpaca, HarmfulQA, HotpotQA) is a bespoke combination rather than a standard, widely recognized safety benchmark, making it harder to compare results to the broader literature or to assess external validity.

strengths: The paper grounds its method in a clean decision-theoretic argument (Theorem 1 and Proposition 1) showing that compound-system utility is minimized near a classifier's decision threshold under mild monotonicity assumptions, giving a principled rationale for boundary-avoiding rewards rather than a purely heuristic method.
The proposed reward (adding |t(x,y) - tau| to a utility term) is simple, practical, and easy to implement within a standard GRPO/LoRA fine-tuning pipeline, lowering the barrier to adoption.

The empirical study is unusually thorough for this class of paper: four base models spanning 0.5B-14B parameters, two model families, multiple reward variants (full reward, guard-only, question-aware), multiple safety classifiers of varying strength, an additional long-context prompt-mix ablation, and a secondary LLM-judge robustness check.

The authors report negative/failure results candidly (e.g., the question-aware reward backfiring, the 0.5B model collapsing into universal refusals under guard-only reward, weak classifiers hurting helpfulness), which strengthens the credibility of the positive findings and avoids overselling.

The related-work section carefully situates the contribution relative to classifier-guided decoding, safety-aligned fine-tuning, and compound-system safety literatures, clarifying what is genuinely new (shifting training rather than inference-time guidance, using the deployment filter itself as the reward signal).
weaknesses: Only a single training run per configuration is reported (Appendix A.1 notes this explicitly, citing compute constraints), so comparisons between reward variants and models rest on one stochastic optimization trajectory each; the reported significance tests capture evaluation-sample variance but not training variance, which is a meaningful reproducibility/soundness gap for RL fine-tuning known to have high run-to-run variability.

The judge-robustness ablation (Appendix D, Table 9) is a genuine threat to the central claim of consistent Pareto improvement: switching from GPT-4.1 to Gemini-2.5 Flash reverses the helpfulness direction for three of four models (helpfulness decreases substantially for Qwen2.5-0.5B, -7B, and Gemma-2-9B), yet the abstract and main results section present the Pareto-improvement finding as robust across settings without adequately foregrounding this sensitivity.

All evaluation relies solely on LLM-as-a-judge scoring for both helpfulness and harmfulness with no human validation, which is a substantive limitation for safety-relevant claims where subtle over-/under-blocking judgments are exactly the phenomenon under study.

No comparison against existing safety-fine-tuning baselines discussed in related work (Safe RLHF, SafeDPO, C-DPO, SACPO, or the safe-completions approach of Yuan et al. 2025 whose evaluation prompts are reused) is provided; the only comparison is fine-tuned vs. base model, leaving open whether boundary guidance outperforms these alternative, more established methods rather than just the unmodified base policy.

The trade-off parameter lambda in the combined reward is fixed (implicitly to 1, per Eq. 1) with no sensitivity analysis, despite the paper's own framing suggesting lambda is an important knob controlling the utility/safety trade-off.

Generation is capped at a short 96-token completion length, which may materially affect both the realism of the benign/helpful responses and the harmfulness of unsafe completions, and this constraint's impact on results is not discussed.

The explicitly flagged future-work item—robustness when the deployment classifier differs from the training-time classifier—is arguably central to whether the method is practically deployable, since safety filters are frequently updated after generator fine-tuning; leaving this entirely unaddressed limits the paper's practical significance.
